entries.title: Parallel batches: the shared pieces for Webster forks and Weaver
entries.brief: DAG batchifier, worktree per batch, merge-back with conflict resolution; open: keeping a fork inside its worktree
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-17)

The pieces parallel batches need are the same whether a batch starts as a Webster fork or as a cold Weaver agent (see `weaver`); only the spawn differs.

1. A DAG batchifier: edges from the cards' targets and `Uses:`, cards joined into batches while the batch graph stays acyclic and under a cost budget, ready batches chosen. New.
2. A worktree per batch, created for the batch and removed after it. New; may build on fabric.
3. Merge-back of each batch worktree into the task branch, with a cheap model such as Haiku resolving textual conflicts. New.
4. The verify on the merged result and its failure ladder. Exists in Webster (verify gate).
5. The batch brackets and report: `begin-batch`, `record-batch`, the changed-files guard and the report contract. Exist in Webster.
6. `plan-dag-view`, to see the graph and the batches. Note filed.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

- Start with these pieces, built so both Webster and Weaver can use them; Webster can run parallel forks first.
- The hard part is getting a Webster fork to work in another worktree than its master's.
- Claude Code's own worktree isolation for agents has given the operator only trouble before.

## Open

How a fork is kept inside its batch's worktree: it inherits the master's working directory and a context full of paths into the task worktree, and `lym` commands find their anchor from the working directory.

### Orch recommendation

Bench before build: a small proof of concept in which one fork is told to work in a worktree Go created, with absolute paths, and a PreToolUse hook refuses its Edit and Write calls outside that worktree, so a slip is refused instead of landing in the wrong tree; measure whether the fork stays inside and what `lym` commands it needs a directory flag for.

entries.title: Every remote operation runs async, and local-only fabric pairs stay an explicit choice only
entries.brief: Remote work goes async except the branch-exists check; batch pairs reach origin like any pair, and the local-only mode stays only as an explicit --local until a use is found or it is removed
entries.body:
## Seen

`batten-start-speed` builds local-only fabric pairs (`fabric add --local`, a local-only branch mark in `gitrepo` with a push refusal, pushes that skip such branches, and local modes of `fabric remove` and `fabric cleanup`): about 630 lines of code, 1360 with tests, plus a local-mark check in the status-push spawn entry.
The mode came from an orch recommendation in `weaver` that batch pairs never reach origin, which was wrong: a batch pair's commits are part of the implementation, and an agent continuing the work on another machine must see what a batch left half done.
The time it saves is small: in the sandbox hub `lym fabric add` took about 1.1 s, nearly all of it two synchronous `git ls-remote` origin probes, with local work about 50 ms and its push already async; `lym fabric remove --remote` took 6 to 7 s of network, at teardown, where nothing waits on it.

## Decisions (operator, 2026-10-18)

- The local-only pair mode stays for now, only as an explicit `fabric add --local` choice, since local work that needs no remote (experiments, local testing) may use it; no lym flow creates local pairs, batch pairs included.
  Remove it (`--local`, the local-only branch mark and its push refusal, the skipped-local reporting in pushes, the local modes of remove and cleanup, and the local-mark check in the status push) if no use turns up.
- Every operation against a remote runs async, so no lym command waits on the network.
  This includes `fabric remove`'s 6 to 7 s of network at teardown (force-with-lease push, archive-tag push, weft branch delete).
- One exception may stay synchronous: the check whether a pair's branches already exist on origin, since a branch found there is fetched and the work continued on, and that is worth waiting for.
  Today that is `fabric add`'s `git ls-remote` probes; they may run in parallel to cut the wait.

## Open

- Which remote operations are synchronous today besides `fabric remove`'s (force-with-lease push, archive-tag push, weft branch delete); an audit of the call sites belongs to the task that builds this.
- How an async remote failure reaches the operator or the orch.

entries.title: Trial: batcher profile wide (budget 300k)
entries.brief: Hub runs a new batcher profile wide, budget 300k; check cost and fork quality before taking it into the template
entries.body:
## Seen

`run-process-ownership` (2026-10-22) ran mostly one card per fork under the `cautious` profile's budget 200k: its cards estimated 145-260k alone.
Measured fork peaks matched the estimates overall; `batch_growth` (7k) is above the ~2k measured when batches go well.
Many small forks were expensive under the identity batcher.

## Decision (operator, 2026-10-22)

`cautious` stays as it is; the hub's `batcher.yaml` adds a profile `wide`, the same as `cautious` but with `budget: 300000`, and makes it `active`.

## Follow-up

After a few loom runs, compare cost and fork quality against earlier runs; then decide whether `wide` goes into `internal/batcher/template.yaml`.

## First check (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

The hub switched at 2026-10-22T15:50 (records commit `216c22a12`); each run's profile comes from its `_lym/webster/state.json`.
Only 2 wide runs with a Webster record have landed (`orch-strand-cycle`, `loom-tail-review`, the latter run on another machine, so no cost data), against 51 cautious runs since 2026-10-15.

| median | cautious (51) | cautious, 10+ cards (18) | wide (2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| cards per fork | 3.0 | 2.1 | 3.1 |
| measured fork peak | 171k | 192k | 310k (1 run) |
| Webster cost per card | $1.15 | $1.50 | $1.12 (1 run) |
| review findings | 1 | 2 | 2 |

- Too few wide runs to decide; no quality regression seen (no stuck batches, one review round).
- In the one measured run, forks of 4-5 cards peaked at 310k and 315k, 31-39% over the batcher's estimate; cautious forks average 0.99 of estimate. If `wide` stays, the estimator needs calibrating above 200k.
- Recheck after 6-8 more wide runs. Rerun with `docs/research/batch-budget-trial-2026-10-24/compare.sh [FROM-date]`; its README and the 2026-10-24 baseline tables sit beside it.

entries.title: Plan writer cost: sub-planners per part, and twill versus a solo writer
entries.brief: The Plan writer is 18% of spend; sub-planners per part for large bundles, and a twill versus solo Opus high comparison on cost, rounds and time
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: the Plan writer is the costliest session type, about $8 per run, $1,306 with its forks over two weeks (18% of all spend).
It averages 81 turns at a mean context of 223k, holds 153k by its first fork and peaks around 308k, mostly from about 71 raw `sed -n`/`grep` code reads.
Every `twill-plan` lens fork inherits that context, about 287k per turn; since 2026-10-20 the writer and its forks cost about $18 per run.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

Fork the lenses earlier, before the code reads pile up, or hand the writer a digest of the code it needs instead of raw reads.
Cutting a quarter of the writer's and its forks' cost saves about 4.5% of all spend; quality must be benched first.

## Discussion with the operator (2026-10-22)

- A code digest instead of raw reads is rejected: it is too inexact unless the code itself is read, and the writer would read the source anyway to be sure.
  Finding what to read is already `relevant.md`'s job; whether the writer uses it is worth measuring (how much of what the writer read the list named).
- Lens forks as fresh agents are rejected: that is the perch itself.
- Sub-planners: Discussion splits the scope into parts in the decision record, groups `relevant.md` per part, and each sub-planner reads only its part; the lead owns the shared spots and joins the card DAG.
  This keeps every review round and matters more as loom tasks are bundled larger.
  Review could split per part the same way, since each fresh reviewer rebuilds its context every round (Plan reviewer: 48 turns at 123k mean context, $2.48 per session).
- Twill-plan versus a solo writer: since the full `twill-plan` fan (2026-10-20), 7 landed loom runs average 2.00 Plan rounds against 2.09 before, while the writer's forks cost about $7 per run and a Plan round about $3.70; too few runs to judge.
  The operator sees strong signs that the twill writer makes a far better one-shot plan in shorter time, and time counts as well as tokens.
  Still, test a solo Opus high writer: compare twill, solo Opus high and solo Fable on Plan cost, Plan rounds and Plan wall time (`lym report timing`) per run.

## Split writing: two variants to bench (operator, 2026-10-22)

Discussion-Write and Plan-Write already run as `shedadapters.MultiLLMProducer` over a `seatengine` table, a chair and advisors; advisors only advise, and twill is the chair forking itself, so today one session writes the whole product.
Two ways to have parts written separately, both benched against each other and against the twill and solo writers before anything reaches production:

1. **Seats with writing assistants.** The chair splits the scope, fixes the interfaces and shared spots, and hands each assistant seat its part; it then joins and checks the parts.
   A new seat role beside the advisor.
   Risks: assistants see neither each other's work nor a shared context, so seams fall to the chair and review, and overlapping parts make several seats read the same code.
2. **Fork-based.** The chair keeps its context lean (scope, split and shared spots only) and forks once per part, so every part writer inherits the same overview without the writer's full reading.
   Technically still one writer with forks, like twill but forking early.

## Data check (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

Plan writer plus its lens forks, means per run (API list price):

| group | runs | writer+forks | forks | Plan-Write wall | Plan rounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before 10-15 (solo writer) | 28 | $9.08 | $0.58 | 16.4 min active | 1.3 |
| 10-15 to 10-19 | 41 | $9.39 | $3.86 | 18.5 min | 1.88 |
| 10-20 to c62274be5 (full twill-plan fan) | 7 | $18.14 | $7.66 | 23.9 min | 2.00 |
| after c62274be5 (five lenses) | 3 | $16.64 | $7.40 | 23.9 min | 1.33 |

- The later groups are larger tasks, so the cost rise is not the fan alone; the five-lens group is too small to judge.
- `relevant.md` use, over 32 runs with a list and a Plan-Write transcript: 85% of named files were read, but only 28% of read files were named (about 3.5 files read per file named, about 7 on large runs). Both shares are lower bounds (directory greps and quarry reads not counted).
- So `relevant.md` works as a floor, not a boundary; most unnamed reading looks like tests and neighbouring callers, which a per-part split of the list would not remove.
- Still open: the solo Opus high and Fable writer bench, and the split-writing variants, which need new runs.
- Scripts, baseline tables and `results.md` are in `docs/research/plan-writer-audit-2026-10-24/`; rerun per its README.

## Discussion versus Plan: double reading (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-25)

55 loom runs seeded 2026-10-15 or later with both a `ly:<slug>:discussion` and a `ly:<slug>:plan` transcript on this machine; cost at API list price from the 10-24 tokencount reports, per run:

| | Discussion | Plan |
|---|---|---|
| phase total (writer, forks, review, fix) | $8.68 | $18.51 |
| writer session alone | $2.07 | $6.60 |
| writer turns / mean context | 39 / 89k tokens | 83 / 183k tokens |
| repo files read by the writer (pooled) | 1,093 | 3,286 |
| share read by both | 62% of Discussion's reads re-read by Plan | 21% of Plan's reads read by Discussion |
| same, without `PATTERN.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `pattern/`, `docs/` | 64% | 20% |

- Discussion costs 0.47 of Plan for the phase and 0.31 for the writer alone; Discussion was the dearer phase in only 4 of 55 runs.
- Plan-Write re-reads about 62% of the files Discussion-Write read (mean of per-run shares 62%), so exploration is repeated, but Plan reads about three times as many files and most of its reading (79%) is new.
- Rough size of the repeat: the Plan-Write reads that Discussion had already made are about 3.3M tokens pooled, about 59k per run (file bytes at current `main` divided by 4; whole files assumed, so an upper bound).
  That is roughly a third of the Plan writer's mean context, and it is paid again on every later turn through the cache.
- File-level only: directory greps, globs and `lym quarry` reads are not counted, and a file is the same file by path, not by the lines read.
- The Discussion phase total holds its review rounds and fixers, which is most of its cost beyond the writer; the segment figures come from the 10-24 tokencount reports, so runs landed since are priced as of then.
- Rerun: `.scratch/discussion-overlap/reads2.sh <slug> plan|discussion` per run, then `analyze.sh`; both stay in `.scratch` and are not committed.
- Decision (operator, 2026-10-25): Discussion stays a separate step; folding it into the Plan writer would add turns to the costliest session.

## Turn audit (landed 2026-10-28)

`docs/research/turn-audit-2026-10-28/report.md` (n = 1 loom run, 213 sessions) finds the Plan writer spends 33 of its 101 turns on serial single-call reads and searches, mostly shell `grep` and `sed -n`, which a merged turn would remove.
It recommends one stencil sentence in `loom-template-plan.md` and in the twill lens directive: issue every search and read you can name in one message.
This is a cheaper cut than the digest, the earlier fork and the split writing above, and the audit proposes no pre-read for the writer.
The recommendation is untested: no run measured the effect, and the Plan row rests on one session.

entries.title: Plan and Discussion fixers on Sonnet, once findings are concrete enough
entries.brief: Webster and Merge fixers are already Sonnet; Plan and Discussion fixers need concrete findings first
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: Opus and Sonnet read cache at the same price, so a swap saves about half a role's non-cache-read cost.
Over the audit window the Plan and Discussion fixers cost about $162 on Opus, the darn writer $45, alignment $40.
The Webster and Merge fixers already run on Sonnet: the template sets `webster_fixer_model` and `merge_fixer_model` to `sonnet[medium]` since `c2d13e5ae` (2026-10-21), so the audit's $37 Opus Webster fixer spend predates that.
`discussion_fixer_model` and `plan_fixer_model` are empty and fall back to `fixer_model`, `opus[medium]`.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-22)

A Sonnet fixer needs findings concrete enough for Sonnet to carry out.
For the Webster perch Sonnet is the natural fit, since Webster's own forks are Sonnet.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

Before the Plan and Discussion fixers move to Sonnet, check that their findings are concrete: each names the place and the change, not only the problem.
A3 (`review-setup-audit`) notes a sloppy fixer causes many late-round defects, and `docs/research/model-downgrade-results.md` holds earlier downgrade results; bench before switching.

## Review-setup audit (landed 2026-10-28)

`docs/research/review-setup-audit-2026-10-28/report.md` is the A3 audit named above.
It does not measure fixer quality or a model swap.
Its finding that bears here: in Plan round 3, 14 of 23 findings point at cards the round-2 fixer left alone, so those late defects are the writer's repository-invariant misses and not a sloppy fixer's; the audit recommends `validate-plan` checks for them.

## Machine checks landed (task `validator-checks`, 2026-10-28)

`lym loom validate-discussion` and `validate-plan`, and the gates that call them, now refuse the recurring findings a machine can see: decision ids and acceptance coverage, missing cited paths and symbols, and in plans `seam-test-unlisted`, `test-tier-unstated` and `doc-go-unlisted`.
That is the audit's recommended `validate-plan` step, so the writer's repository-invariant misses are caught before a review round; the fixer-quality question here is unchanged and still needs a bench.

entries.title: Large tasks: Discussion, a pre-planner, and the pieces as darn runs inside the task's beam
entries.brief: Discussion decides scope, a pre-planner splits it into contracted pieces, each piece runs as darn from the task's beam, a whole-task perch reviews, then align and land
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-22)

A large task runs as a tapestry whose implementation is a set of darn runs inside its own beam:

1. Task A runs Discussion as today; Discussion stays the one agent that talks with the operator and decides scope.
2. A pre-planner breaks the decided scope into smaller pieces that together make up the whole scope.
   Each piece gets a contract: what it takes in, the behaviour it delivers, the names it exports to other pieces, and which pieces it depends on; not the inside, which the darn finds itself.
3. Each piece becomes a darn task with that contract and its part of the decision record and `relevant.md`, with `depends_on` between pieces.
4. The next producer turns Task A's worktree into a beam.
5. The darn tasks run from beam A as ordinary darn runs and merge back into Task A's branch, not `main`; pieces with no dependency between them run in parallel.
6. When every darn has merged back, a Task A-wide perch reviews the whole and makes small fixes.
7. The rest is as today: Parent-Align, PR, landing, so `main` takes Task A whole.

## Why

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: a loom run carries a fixed cost of about $23, mostly Plan and the review rounds, and the Plan writer reads about 250k of context before it writes (91% of its peak).
Darn's fixed cost is about $2.60.
Split this way, each darn reads only its piece once, plans and implements it, and is reviewed by its own perch; Discussion and the whole-task perch keep loom's scope and overall check.
It came out of discussing sub-planners for the Plan writer (note `plan-writer-context`): pieces small enough to plan and implement together are darn runs.

## Depends on

The beam setup: `orch-any-worktree` is landed (dd11ab09f: beams, pairs from a parent pair, `lym beam create`, `land`; its `promote` was removed by `beam-start-and-ownership`, which also added `lym beam start` and the `pawl` recipe), and `umbrella-daemon` is landed too (c2a03a885: dobby, a per-beam daemon that drives runs).
Earlier wording: `orch-any-worktree` (umbrella tasks spawning and landing from their own worktree) and `umbrella-daemon` (a daemon per beam that drives its runs).

## Open

- Contract precision: too loose and pieces collide, too tight and the pre-planner becomes today's Plan writer.
- A darn that finds its contract wrong stops and escalates to Task A instead of improvising; dependent pieces wait.
- What drives the darns inside the beam: dobby now starts and drives a beam's ready tasks (c2a03a885); open is how Task A's run waits for them.
- How large the whole-task perch's fixes may be before they mean a piece failed.
- Quality against full loom: each piece gets one perch instead of Plan and Webster review; measure follow-up fixes against loom runs.
- Cost: Discussion, pre-planner, N darns and the whole-task perch against a loom run of the same size.

## Review placement (operator, 2026-10-22)

- The pre-plan gets a perch, but the pre-plan is far smaller than today's plan format: pieces and their contracts, not cards.
- No perch per darn: a review per batch proved far too expensive in Millhouse, and a perch per piece is the same.
  The pieces run as darn with review off (`code_max_bounces: 0`, since `code-review-one-perch` made darn's perch the Code-Review perch), each still passing its own gate and tests; the whole-task perch after the last merge-back is the code review, as Webster's round over the whole diff is today.
  For scale, a darn perch costs about $1.30 per run in the audit window.
- The pieces run tests as they go, the way Webster's card gate runs after every card.

## Piece recipe `stitch` (operator, 2026-10-22)

The pieces run on their own recipe, `stitch`, derived from darn, not on a darn profile: rows go away, not only bounds.
Alignment per piece is pointless when the piece is a closed, synchronised share of an umbrella that is aligned whole.

- Kept: Preflight; the writer, on Sonnet, briefed by its pre-plan contract.
- Dropped: Code-Bouncer and the Code-Burler review/fix rows (review off), Describe and PR-Review.
  Since `loom-tail-review` (2026-10-24) darn has no Merge-In, Publish, PR-Align or PR-Gate rows; its Finalize merges the parent in under the lock.
- Finalize merges into the umbrella branch under the parent lock instead of landing on `main`.
- Friction-Reflect runs once per umbrella, not per piece.
- A `stitch` task runs only inside an umbrella; it cannot run alone.
- Estimate (orch, not measured): about $2-2.50 per piece against about $6 for a darn with review.

Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-24): once `stitch` exists, Codex could run the pre-planner, as a role apart from the Claude-written code (see note `codex-engine`).

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-23): darn itself as the piece implementer

Once `loom-tail-review` has landed, darn itself may serve as the pieces' implementer, since that task removes much of the run tail's ceremony, such as the pull request.
Whether `stitch` then stays a recipe of its own, or becomes darn with the tail rows a piece does not need turned off, is to be weighed against what `loom-tail-review` lands.

## Test depth of a piece (operator, 2026-10-23)

A piece run does not run the full suite a standalone darn runs before it lands.
The umbrella runs the full suite once, after every piece has merged back.
Which tiers a piece's own gates run is open; the gate key per recipe row is stated in `internal/gateslot`'s doc (`gate-runs-once`, landed): a piece's rows read `darn-write`, `code-burler-fix` and `finalize`.

## Pre-plan depth (orch, 2026-10-24, not decided)

- A coarse pre-plan leaves design to the pieces, so each piece needs an Opus writer.
- A detailed pre-plan carries the design, so Sonnet pieces may do, at the cost of a heavier pre-planner.
- Pieces cannot be counted on to run in parallel: `tools/plandag/plandag.sh` on `loom-tail-review`'s plan found 52 cards, a critical path of 20 and a mean parallelism of 2.6.
  A beam's gain is then mostly smaller review scopes, not wall time.

entries.title: A task that turns out to be a project is refiled as a project, keeping its Discussion findings
entries.brief: The agent files a note with its findings and tells the orch; the operator decides, then the run ends and a new beam spawns from the parent
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-25, operator 2026-10-30)

A beam is made from a project entry with `lym beam create`, and its life is one batten run over that entry with the `pawl` recipe.
`lym beam promote` is removed: switching a running task's worktree into a beam halfway proved messy.
A task can still turn out too large while its Discussion runs, and then it has to become a project instead.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-30)

The agent that finds this out, in Discussion or in a research or darn run, files a note on the board with everything it found, tells its parent, the orch, and ends its turn.
It never files a project or a task, and starts nothing: only the operator decides what becomes a task or a project.
The orch puts the finding to the operator; when the operator decides on a project, the old run ends and the project is created and spawned as a new beam from the parent, never from the old task's worktree.
Nothing is switched in place.

The note must keep what the agent learned: its body holds the Discussion writer's findings and decisions, so they become the beam's starting design and are not left behind in the old run's records history.
Note `loom-beam-darns` is a related shape, where a large tapestry task turns into a beam and runs its pieces as darn runs inside it.

## Open design points

- How the agent tells its parent: a message to the orch with the note's slug, and whether the run stops by itself afterwards or waits for the orch to end it.
- How the run ends once the operator has decided: the orch ends it with `lym batten cancel <slug> --remove`.
- How the note becomes the project entry and its beam: the orch turns it into a project entry after the operator's go-ahead and runs `lym beam create`, with the old task's entry removed or marked superseded in the same step.
- Whether the old run's code commits, if any, are kept or dropped.
- With dobby as the only driver of a beam's runs (only beams have a dobby, and the prime is the root beam), a worktree that is to have worktrees under it must be a beam from the start, so this route is the only way a task's scope grows into a tree of runs.

entries.title: A run keeps the lym binary and Bolt instructions it started with
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-27)

A run reads its instructions live while it runs: the `lym` binary, and the stencils, specs and hub config on Bolt (`_board/_lym/{stencils,specs,config}`).
A landing deploys a new `lym` and can change those files, so a run started on one version can finish on another, such as a darn run that sat between its drift rows when `darn-drift-await-row` landed and its recipe changed under it (that landing wrote no transition code: such a run halts at Drift-Verify and is settled by hand with `lym drift waive`).
LoomYard takes no special care for such a run today, and the operator wants none written per change (operator, 2026-10-27).

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-27)

A run keeps the version it started with, so nothing changes under it.
- Bolt: the run records the Bolt commit at its start and reads stencils, specs and config from that commit through git, in the one place those files are read, instead of from the working files; no copy is made.
- Binary: at the run's start the running `lym` is copied into a store under a name derived from its content, as the gate's prebuilt store does (`internal/gateslot`), and the run's driver and agents call that copy.
- Shared state stays live: the board, locks, gate slots, creel mail and the run's own records.
- One verb moves a run onto the newest version, for a run that needs a fix that landed after it started.

## Open

- Shared daemons (dobby, creel, gate) run the newest binary, so a pinned run's formats must stay readable by them, and a pinned binary must not write the board in an older format.
- Plugins and skills are loaded by Claude Code from one shared place and are left out of the first step.

entries.title: A window lym opens is snapped into the active desktop tiling by a configured command
entries.brief: After opening a window lym runs a machine-local configured command, such as the operator tiling script; lym knows nothing about KDE
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-28)

The operator runs KDE Plasma with virtual desktops and tiling.
The Konsole windows lym opens on a run's worktree (`lym reed window`, batten's terminal for each run) and the VS Code windows it opens (`lym ide`) land wherever KWin puts them, untiled and on the current desktop, so the operator moves and tiles each by hand.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-31)

Lym places no window itself: the operator's own tiling script does it.
Neve's `~/.local/bin/arrange-to-tiles.sh` (Meta+Alt+A, run through xremap) fills the active desktop's existing Custom Tiling grid with the windows on it, without changing the grid's shape.
- A machine-local config key names a command lym runs after it opens a window, such as `~/.local/bin/arrange-to-tiles.sh`: after a run's terminal window, `lym reed window` and `lym ide`.
- The window lands on the active desktop, as KWin puts it today, and the command snaps it into the grid.
- Lym knows nothing about KDE: with the key unset nothing runs, and each machine names its own script (OSL-1046 runs Plasma 5).
- Lym runs the command only once the new window is mapped, or after a short wait, so the script sees it.

entries.title: Prove the dotnet scoper, shared build and Drift on the C# sandbox hub
entries.brief: Switch the sandbox gate to scoper dotnet, a build step and --no-build, then enable Drift there
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-29)

The sandbox hub `lym-csharp-LYMHUB` (shortname `cs`, anchor `lym-csharp/dotnet`, over `Knatte18/lym-csharp`) ran its first darn run, `friction-colebrook`, end to end, and it landed as `7f50ffe`.
Its gate is the simple form: `tier0` runs `dotnet test` without `Category=Slow` and `tier1` with it, with no `scoper`, no `build` step and no `--no-build`.
So the dotnet scoper, the shared build and Drift are not proved on a C# repository.
The first `tier1` gate run on Neve died with "Internal CLR error (0x80131506)" after 900 s and passed on a rerun; the cause is unknown.

## Idea

Switch the sandbox gate to `scoper: dotnet`, a `build` step and `--no-build`, so the scoper and the shared build are proved there, then turn on `drift.enabled` there to prove Drift, before any C# hub that holds proprietary code relies on them.
The hub's setup is in `docs/dotnet-hub.md`; the sandbox stays the place to reproduce a lym fault another C# hub shows.

entries.title: Creel mail between hubs through an inbox folder, with a verified sender
entries.brief: A shared inbox folder takes mail from other hubs; each file names the sender hub and agent so a reply knows where to go
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

The operator sometimes has the orch write straight into another repository, such as Scribe or Quarry, and would rather let the orchs of the hubs talk to each other, which is how lym is meant to be used.
Creel has no support for this today.
One daemon serves one hub, its socket is named from the hub path, and the hub a call reaches is the hub of the directory it runs from.
A process outside the hub's strands is `EXTERNAL`, shown with a terminal and parent-process envelope, and its replies reach only a waiting `post --wait-reply`.
`EXTERNAL` is the wrong sender for this: the receiver must see the real strand that sent the message.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-30)

A shared inbox folder takes in messages from outside the hub.
The file a message becomes carries its sender: the path of the sender hub's inbox folder and the name of the agent that sent it.
A message needs a receiver, so the daemon knows whom to give it to.
A reply is addressed from those two fields, so the replier knows which agent in which hub to answer.

## Verifying the sender (operator, 2026-10-30)

A file cannot prove its sender: any process of the same user can write one, so a prompt-injected agent could write `ly:orch` in the sender field.
The sending daemon, which reads the caller from `SO_PEERCRED` as it does today, writes the file.
The receiving daemon then asks the sending hub's daemon to confirm it:

1. The file names the sender hub's path, and the receiver derives that hub's socket name from it, as `creel-<shortname>-<hash>.sock`, with no registry.
2. The receiver sends one call in creel's JSON-lines protocol, such as `confirm`, with the message id, the receiver and a hash of the text.
3. The sender's daemon looks in its own journal for a message from that strand to that receiver with that hash, and answers yes or no, never the text.
4. Only on yes does the receiver show the sender as that strand; otherwise the message shows as unverified.

This is a call and not a signature on the file, since a signature needs a secret and every agent of the same user can read a secret file; the sending daemon cannot be fooled, because it reads its caller from the process and knows what it sent.
A message can be confirmed once, so a copied file cannot be reused.
The journal's retention bounds how late a confirmation can come, so the receiver confirms when the message arrives.
A sending daemon that is down is started as a client starts it today, or the message stays unverified.
The check works only within one user, since the sockets do.

## Open design points

- Where the folder lives and how a sender addresses a hub: a path derived from the hub path, like the socket, and a record on the machine that maps a shortname to a hub path.
- What a reply does across the hub border: it goes to the sender's inbox folder, addressed to the agent the file names.
- How a role treats mail from another hub: as data to weigh, never as the operator's instruction, since it is a channel for prompt injection into the receiving orch.
- How this fits a closed area for lym's process tree (research note `sandboxing-options-2026-10-30`): the folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.
- Another machine: a folder that a synced directory carries would reach a hub on Neve; not designed here.

entries.title: A closed area for lym: bwrap sandbox in stages, off by default
entries.brief: Run the lym process tree in a bwrap area with a host proxy and broker, built in three stages with a stop; to be split if it goes ahead
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

Every agent lym starts runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which many people do not accept, and a repository that states it supports safe sandboxing is worth more than one that does not.
The operator uses lym alone, on Linux (OSL-1046: Ubuntu 24.04; Neve: Kubuntu on Ubuntu 26.04, Plasma 6), and has no interest in other users or in Windows.
The research is `docs/research/sandboxing-options-2026-10-30.md`: it weighs `bwrap`, Landlock, a dedicated Linux user, systemd sandboxing, podman and Claude Code's own `/sandbox`, and the packages and cards each would change.

Two exposures hold today with no area: an agent can reach `/run/user/<uid>/bus` and through it `systemd-run --user`, which starts any process outside lym's tree, and it can type into other hubs' tmux panes through their sockets in `/tmp/tmux-<uid>`, the Models hub's among them.

## Idea

Run the whole lym process tree inside a `bwrap` area launched by lym itself, with the agents free inside it and a short, controlled list of exits.
It is an option the operator turns on, never a requirement: with it off, everything works as it does today, and with it on, nothing starts when the sandbox cannot.
The operator thinks the full design is complicated and error-prone, and doubts it will work without large problems, so it is built in stages with a stop between them.
This is one large note and is split into tasks, or a project, only when the operator decides it goes ahead.

### Before the area: two cheap steps

- Start a hub's tmux server from a Konsole window, not a VS Code terminal: the server inherits the `vscode` AppArmor profile, which grants user namespaces to every agent of the hub.
- A line in `README.md` that every agent lym starts runs with bypass permissions, and that lym belongs on a machine the operator is willing to hand to its agents.

### Stage 1: the filesystem area only

`bwrap` with `--unshare-all --die-with-parent --clearenv` around reed's tmux server and everything under it, started by a new `lym area start` and a supervisor inside.

- The hub is bound read-write at its own path, since the tmux server name, the creel socket name, git's worktree links and Claude Code's transcript directory all derive from absolute paths; `/usr`, `/etc` and `/opt` are read-only, `$HOME` a tmpfs with read-only binds of the Go toolchain, the Claude Code binary and the installed `lym`.
- The area has its own Claude config directory and Go caches bound at the usual paths, with the host's plugin cache read-only on top, so the host's `settings.json` hooks never run in it.
- One host directory holds the tmux socket directory, so `lym reed attach` from outside drives the server inside; tried on OSL-1046 with a tmux server inside `bwrap`.
- `.git/hooks` is read-only; `.git/config` stays writable, since `internal/gitrepo/branchmark.go` writes `branch.<b>.lymLocal` into it.
- Network stays open and there is no broker, so the landing deploy, `lym reed window`, `lym ide` and `lym hibernate request` do not work from inside; the operator does them by hand, from outside.
- A config module `area` with `required`, off by default; `lym area start` refuses on any failure and never falls back to an unsandboxed start.
- Ubuntu 24.04 needs a one-time AppArmor profile for `/usr/bin/bwrap`, loaded by root; the report names the profile, and Ubuntu 25.04 and later ship it, which is not verified on Neve.

This closes the two exposures above and shows early whether tmux, creel and dobby run well inside an area.

### Stop: the operator decides whether stage 1 works well enough to go on.

### Stage 2: egress through a host proxy

No network inside the area; a host-side proxy, reached through a bound socket, allows CONNECT to `api.anthropic.com`, `claude.ai`, `platform.claude.com`, `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`, `github.com` and `api.github.com`, with a loopback relay inside the area.
Telemetry and the auto-updater are off by environment.
The GitHub token handed to the area is fine-grained and limited to the hub's repositories; the operator's `gh` login never enters.
WebFetch and the `prowler` skill reach only these hosts.

### Stage 3: a broker for the remaining exits

A host-side process serving a fixed set of verbs and never a command line from the area: the landing deploy (it fetches `origin/main` into its own clone, checks the commit is the tip, builds with the host's Go and installs), `lym reed window` opening Konsole, and `lym hibernate request`.
`lym ide` is refused, since VS Code on the host would run git over repositories the area writes; the host runs no git over the area's repositories at all.

## What is not claimed

Isolation from a kernel exploit, which needs a virtual machine; that data in the area cannot leave through an allowed host; and that a landed change of lym itself cannot run on the host once deployed, which matters on this hub because it develops lym.
Landlock stays a possible inner layer once both machines run a kernel with ABI 9 and 10, and Claude Code deny rules in shuttle's settings are a cheap second line inside the area; the dedicated user, podman, systemd sandboxing and Claude Code's `/sandbox` inside lym runs are left out.
The report estimates the whole at five tasks and eighteen cards.

## Related

Note `creel-cross-hub-mail`: the inbox folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.

entries.title: pr-continue wakes the PR-Review wait at once
entries.brief: The PR-Review wait sleeps up to a minute between wakes, so lym loom pr-continue takes effect up to a minute late
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-30)

On the first PR-Review run, the reviewer agent ran `lym loom pr-continue` and the run went on only after a while.
The wait sleeps between wakes, from a floor of one second up to a ceiling of one minute while nothing changes (`prWaitFloor`, `prWaitCeiling` in `internal/landingshed/prreview.go`), and `pr-continue` only sets a flag that the next wake reads.
Finalize's gate then runs on the landed tree as for any landing, which takes minutes by itself.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-30)

`lym loom pr-continue` wakes the waiting row at once, so the PR is closed and Finalize begins with no wait of up to a minute.

entries.title: A seed says only that a run starts at its start, with no producer name
entries.brief: The shared seed names Preflight as the first producer for every recipe; the seed should name none, and the recipe supplies its first row.
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

A new beam stopped at once because the shared seed set its status file's `current_producer` to `Preflight`, a row the pawl recipe lacked.
The seed names the producer an inner run starts at, so each recipe's first row must match a name hard-coded in `loomshed.Seed` (`internal/loomshed/seed.go`), which the bootstrap shared by every inner recipe calls.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-30)

- The seed names no producer: it says only that the run starts at its start, and the recipe's first row is the start.
- A seed can then never name a row its recipe lacks, whatever recipe a run is seeded for.
- The change reaches the shared seeding for tapestry, darn and pawl, how the status file records the current producer before the first pass, and the verbs that move a run (`goto`, resume), which the task checks.

entries.title: Landing commits drop Co-Authored-By and Lym-Task, and carry an optional credit listing the engines used
entries.brief: Replace the per-engine Co-Authored-By line and the Lym-Task line with one optional credit block that lists the LLM services the task used.
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

A landing commit ends with `Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>`, from `engine_trailers.claude` in the landing config (`internal/landingshed/template.yaml`), and a Codex run would add `Co-Authored-By: Codex` the same way.
That makes each engine a co-author of the commit, which the operator does not want.
The commit's last line is `Lym-Task: <slug>`, added by `taskTrailer` in `internal/landingshed/finalize.go`; the operator sees no reason for it.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-30 and 2026-10-31)

- No engine is credited as a co-author: no `Co-Authored-By` line for Claude, Codex or any other engine.
- `Lym-Task: <slug>` is removed.
  A landing commit and its pull request carry no trace of LoomYard or of its use, bar the credit below.
- The commit ends with a credit block, written as plain lines, never as git trailers, by default:

  ```
  Created using
   - LoomYard https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard
   - Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
   - Codex <codex@openai.com>
  ```

- Each line is a config text of its own in the landing config: the heading, the LoomYard line, and one line per engine.
- The LoomYard line is always in the block.
- An engine's line appears only when that engine ran a session in the task, detected automatically as `engine_trailers` decides today; an engine that ran nothing in the task is not listed.
- The same block serves the pull request's body, so a commit and its pull request carry one signature.

entries.title: One verb to take work over on another machine, leaving every run in a known state
entries.brief: Moving to another machine is many hand steps, and afterwards run states are unclear
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

Moving work from one machine to another is a string of hand steps, and afterwards the operator cannot tell what state the runs are in.
On 2026-10-31 the operator moved from OSL-1046 to Neve: `lym fabric pull`, `lym s`, a `lym adopt` whose tier0 check mailed the orch, and more by hand.
Task `dobby-land-notice-needs-flag` had started on OSL-1046 on 2026-10-30 and stood at `running · Code-Bouncer`, unlanded.
After the move, dobby on Neve reported its driver strand dead, then a fresh Go driver took it on, and neither the operator nor the orch could say at once whether the run was finished, should run or should not.

The run went on because `lym adopt` resumes it: step 6 of its help resumes each moved run not done as a detached first pass, so adopting is also starting.
Bolt itself is reconciled with origin first by each of `lym fabric pull`, `lym adopt` (its step 1) and `lym beam start`, so the board was current; what was missing is a view of the runs.

## Idea

One verb takes a machine over and leaves it in a known state, in place of the hand steps.
- It pulls warp and weft, adopts the runs and beams the operator names, and starts the dobby and orch, each step idempotent.
- It starts no run by itself: every adopted run stays held until the operator lets it go on, so nothing runs that the operator does not expect.
- It prints one line per run: landed, running here, held for a go-ahead, or owned by another machine, with the row it stands at.

## Open

- Which steps the move took on 2026-10-31 in full; the operator's account is the source.
- Whether the old machine releases its runs first, by a verb of its own, before the new one adopts them.

entries.title: sampler: an interactive loom recipe, the operator iterating with an agent in the run's worktree until done
entries.brief: A Shed recipe whose agent waits for the operator and iterates on the result, then lands as usual
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

Some work needs many rounds between the operator and an agent on the result itself, and a one-shot writer makes it badly: a README written as a teaching text (task `readme-rewrite`), the board's README (note `board-viewer`), and trying out the reed status bar's buttons (note `reed-status-buttons`).
Darn's writer is non-interactive, and tapestry's `discussion_interactive` only interviews the operator before anything is written.

## Idea

A new loom recipe, `sampler`, beside `tapestry` and darn, under the loom contract `run-verbs-shared` builds: an interactive agent the operator iterates with in the run's own worktree.
Batten stays the same for it as for every recipe.

- The record is written mechanically from the board entry, as darn's is without Discussion; what the operator and the agent settle on the way the agent appends with `lym loom decision add`, so Describe and any review measure against it.
- The build segment is the interactive agent alone.
- Batten makes the worktree, opens the window and starts the agent with the task's body as its brief; the agent waits for the operator in its pane.
- The operator and the agent go as many rounds as the operator wants; the agent commits as it goes.
- The operator tells the agent the work is done, and the agent runs a `lym` verb that ends the build segment, as the PR-Review agent runs `lym loom pr-continue` when the operator says so.
- The run then goes on as usual: the Code-Review perch, off by default, then Describe, Finalize and Land.
- The result is one of:
  - a change to the repository, such as the README or `docs/`, landed as an ordinary commit;
  - an entry on the board, written by the agent through `lym board`, in which case the run has no commits and lands empty, which lym already supports;
  - a trial, as `reed-status-buttons` needs, in which case the run can use a tmux server of its own, so that what it tries does not disturb the operator's strands.

## The agent (operator, 2026-10-31)

The agent is not Discussion-Write: Discussion-Write's stencil binds it to explore the code, ask and write the decision record, never to make the work itself.
This agent makes the result with the operator, and gets a short stencil of its own: stay in the run's worktree, commit as it goes, and write board results through `lym board`.
It shares only the mechanism with Discussion-Write's interactive mode: an interactive shuttle session (`lym shuttle run --interactive`) in a pane that waits for the operator.

## Waiting on the operator (operator, 2026-10-31)

While the agent waits for the operator, dobby's quiet notice and shuttle's idle timeout are off for this recipe.
A run is started only when the operator means to work with it.

## Name (operator, 2026-10-31)

The recipe is named `sampler`: a weaver's sampler is the cloth patterns are tried and adjusted on.

entries.title: Finalize settles a rejected fixer change in place and never sends the run back
entries.brief: A fix review loop inside Finalize that escalates at its cap, in place of on_reroute
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

Finalize still sends a run back in one case: when its merge fixer spent its cap, or made an over-cap change, and Finalize's own solo fix review does not approve that change.
tapestry's Finalize then reroutes to Parent-Align and darn's to Code-Bouncer (`on_reroute` in `contracts/recipes/tapestry-recipe.yaml` and `darn-recipe.yaml`), bounded by Shed's reroute cap.
The operator does not want a run bounced back to earlier rows, and a halt handed to the orch helps no one either, since the orch can do little with it: the run must settle it itself.

## Idea

Finalize settles a fixer change in place, under the parent lock, and never reroutes.
- A fix review that does not approve hands its findings to the fixer, which fixes them in place, and the review checks again: a small perch inside Finalize.
- The loop has a cap; at the cap Finalize escalates with the unresolved findings, as a review loop that ran out of rounds does, and the operator decides.
  The operator can accept the change as it stands, and the run then lands with the unresolved findings written into the change description, as `lym loom circling accept` does for a review loop.
- Parent-Align and Code-Review are not run again, and `on_reroute` goes from Finalize in every recipe.

entries.title: Merge in from parent as a task of its own in a beam, in place of pawl's perch round
entries.brief: A ready-made command starts a run that brings the parent into a beam, with Drift; pawl drops its own Code-Review perch
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

The pawl recipe, a beam's run, has a Code-Review perch of its own: when the beam lands, Parent-Align brings the parent in and the perch reviews the beam's whole diff (`contracts/recipes/pawl-recipe.yaml`).
The operator does not want pawl to have its own perch round: the beam's members are already reviewed by their own runs.

## Idea

Bringing the parent into a beam is a task of its own: a run with its own worktree inside the beam's project, "merge in from parent".
- It is a ready-made command the operator or the orch starts with one call, at any time, not only at landing.
- The run merges the parent into the beam, settles conflicts and gate failures with the merge fixer, and can run Drift.
- pawl then lands the beam without a perch round of its own.

## Open

- The command's name and where it lives (`lym beam ...`).
- Whether pawl starts such a run itself before it lands, or requires one to have landed since the parent last moved.

entries.title: Pawl becomes a loom recipe, with a project decision record and no review rounds
entries.brief: Pawl joins the loom contract; a project record written at beam create and changed only through decision add
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

Pawl takes one board entry, a project, and ends with its beam merged into the parent, as a loom recipe takes a task and lands it.
It has no decision record: its Code-Review perch compares against a snapshot of the project's board entry, and `lym loom decision add` cannot change a beam's scope.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-31)

Pawl becomes a loom recipe under the contract `run-verbs-shared` builds, with the members' runs in the writer's place.
Its Code-Review rounds are zero: pawl has no review round of its own (the note `parent-merge-task` replaces the perch).

Pawl gets a decision record that holds only what binds the whole project: its goal, its bounds and the constraints every member follows.
It is no log of what landed; git and the board hold that, and a member landing never touches it.
- `lym beam create` writes it mechanically: the project entry's body verbatim under `## Goal`, every other section empty.
- After that only a scope change touches it, through `lym loom decision add <beam-slug>`, which the beam's own orch runs.
- `decision add` on a beam tells the live agents of every member run under it that the project record holds a new decision.
- Each member's Discussion and writer read the project record as constraints, and the beam's Describe reads it when the beam lands.

lym enforces the route:
- Once a project has a record, `lym board upsert` refuses a change to its body and names `lym loom decision add <beam-slug>`, as the board already refuses scope edits on a run-held task.
- The orch role lym ships says that a beam's scope change goes through `decision add` on the beam.

entries.title: An idle interactive run saves its work and pauses, to go on another time
entries.brief: lym asks an idle interactive agent to commit what it has and end, and the run resumes later
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

An interactive run (task `interactive-recipe`) waits for the operator in its pane, and has dobby's quiet notice and shuttle's idle timeout off while it does.
Since lym runs the agent, it can watch how long the agent has waited.

## Idea

When the agent has been idle for a set time, lym asks it to write down what it has, commit it, and end its session; the run pauses, and the operator picks it up another time with the agent resumed from that state.

entries.title: The hibernate request is carried by dobby, not a daemon of its own
entries.brief: Move lym hibernate request into dobby, once dobby and hibernate share the past-Land test
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

`lym hibernate request` runs a daemon of its own that waits for the runs to land and every session to pause before it hibernates the machine.
Dobby already drives every run of its worktree to its end, and `landing-watch` gives dobby and the hibernate daemon one shared test for a run past its Land row.

## Idea

The hibernate request moves into dobby, so no daemon of its own waits on the runs.

## Open

- A request spans every beam, since `--after-all` waits on all runs while a dobby sees only its own: which dobby carries it, or how the dobbies agree.
- A hub pause must leave the dobby that waits outside it.

entries.title: Rename the Bolt checkout directory _board to _bolt, by script alone
entries.brief: A pure, mechanical rename of _board to _bolt everywhere, with a rename program for existing hubs
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

The hub's Bolt checkout is the directory `_board`, but it holds far more than the board: `board.json`, its README and design files, the hub's `_lym` config and orch rules, and soon heddle's database.
The name says board where the directory is Bolt.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-31)

A pure rename of `_board` to `_bolt`, the name of the repository it checks out, done mechanically by script and nothing else.
- Every spelling of `_board` becomes `_bolt`: the constants (`fabricengine.BoardDirName`, the copy in `lymcwd`, `runproc.HubOwner`), user-facing messages, comments, tests, stencils, the `ly:board` skill and docs.
- Existing hubs on Neve and OSL-1046 have `_board` on disk, so the task ships a rename program as `tapestry-rename` had, run once per hub.
  It also re-points everything that holds an absolute path into `_board`, such as config, stored reed commands and VS Code setup, and refuses to run while any lym process or run is alive.
- No compatibility: lym itself knows `_bolt` only, with no fallback to `_board`, no detection of the old name and no migration case in its code, since no run on the old name meets the new binary (operator, 2026-10-31).
  The one-shot rename program is the only place the old name appears.
- The rename program stays short, with no what-if code (operator, 2026-10-31): it handles the hubs on Neve and OSL-1046 as they are today, stops and says what it found when anything looks other than expected, leaving that to be fixed by hand, and is deleted from the repository once both hubs are migrated.
- No refactor rides along: splitting a `BoltDirName` from `BoardDirName` and routing every spelling through one constant belong to another task.
- It runs alone, with no other run in flight.

entries.title: Comment cleanup: parallel agents fix stale comments across the repository
entries.brief: An orchestrating agent hands each package to a worker, possibly Haiku 5.5, that fixes comments no longer true or pinning perishable specifics
entries.body:
## Seen (operator and hub orch, 2026-10-31)

Comments in the Go source go stale as the code moves on.
Two found today: `internal/fabricengine/weftwiring.go` still speaks of a future `_lym/raddle/` squash-merge-back, though raddle will never be built; and many comments spell the `_board` path instead of naming its constant (note `bolt-dir-rename`).
There are surely more, in every package, against `scribe:prose`'s rule never to pin a perishable specific.

## Idea

A comment-cleanup campaign over the whole repository.
- A worker fixes each comment or text that no longer matches the code, names something gone or planned and dropped, or pins a perishable specific: a count, a list of current callers, a path or name spelled where a constant or identifier should be named.
- Workers change comments and text only, never code.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-31)

- One darn run, whose agent orchestrates the whole campaign: it splits the work and spawns the workers, many in parallel; not one darn per package, which would be far too many runs.
- Scope: Go comments and docstrings, each package's `doc.go`, the stencils and the docs.
- Models by scope: Haiku 5.5 takes the comments and docstrings of code files, being fast and cheap while its context stays under about 100k, which one package's read fits; `doc.go`, stencils and docs need a stronger model, Sonnet 5.5, as the `docs` profile's writer is.
- No review step of its own: most comments are assumed sound, and this run is itself the check on them; the darn's usual Code-Review is enough.

Related: note `hardener` is another autonomous campaign run by an orchestrating agent.

## Open

- How the orchestrating agent spawns its workers under lym, with Haiku 5.5 as their model.

entries.title: A finished run blocked at Worktree-Teardown with its pair gone can be neither retried nor cancelled
entries.brief: batten run refuses a teardown retry with no pair worktree, though the pair removal already succeeded and only the remote branch delete is left
entries.body:
## Seen (hub orch, 2026-10-31)

Run `pawl-starts-at-preflight` landed on OSL-1046 on 2026-10-30, and its Worktree-Teardown removed the pair but failed to delete the remote weft branch `pawl-starts-at-preflight-weft`: GitHub answered the `git push --delete` with an Internal Server Error.
The run stayed `blocked` at Worktree-Teardown, and its error said "resume this run to retry the deletion".
On Neve a day later, `lym batten run pawl-starts-at-preflight` refused before the retry: `origin reconcile of run pawl-starts-at-preflight: no pair worktree /home/knatte/Code/loomyard-LYMHUB/pawl-starts-at-preflight`.
The pair was already removed, so the way forward the error named can never work, on either machine.

Workaround used: the remote weft branch was deleted by hand (its commit is kept by the tag `archive/pawl-starts-at-preflight/6c0f8a26a141`); ending the run then failed, as below.

## Expected

A Worktree-Teardown retry whose pair is already removed skips the origin reconcile that needs the pair and retries only what is left, here the remote branch deletion, on any machine.
The way forward a teardown error names must be one that works.

## Deadlock (hub orch, 2026-10-31)

After the remote branch was deleted by hand, `lym batten cancel pawl-starts-at-preflight` refused too: "the work of pawl-starts-at-preflight reached its parent; way forward: run lym batten run pawl-starts-at-preflight to finish the landing", which is the verb that refuses for want of the pair.
`lym batten cleanup` removes only done runs' records, so no verb can end the run, and it stays `blocked` at Worktree-Teardown in dobby's overview.

entries.title: The appended system prompt states the gate rule once, not twice
entries.brief: The raw-go and refuse-raw deny notices both carry the full gate rule into every session
entries.body:
## Seen (hub orch, 2026-10-31)

The deny notices shuttle appends to every Claude session's system prompt carry the whole gate rule twice.
The raw go row (`raw-go` in `internal/shellguard/rows.go`) and the refuse-raw row each end in the same text, from "Gate rule: run lym gate test in the foreground" to "so the prompt cache stays warm between calls", so a session reads it twice in its system prompt.

## Idea

State the gate rule once in the appended notice, and let the second row's notice say only what it refuses.
Each row's steer, the reason shown when a call is denied, keeps the full rule, since a denied call needs the way forward at hand.

entries.title: The orch resume pointer arrives twice after a compact cycle
entries.brief: hookDelivered compares the hook mark with the compaction boundary, which is stamped after the hook ran
entries.body:
## Seen

After a requested compact cycle of the orch (2026-10-31), the resume pointer reached the session twice: once as SessionStart hook context and once typed by the watcher.

- The hook runs `orchengine.ResumeContext` (`internal/orchengine/resumecontext.go`), which writes the resume mark with `At` from the hook's own clock.
- The watcher's skip check `hookDelivered` (`internal/orchengine/watcher.go`) counts the pointer delivered only when `mark.At` is not before `st.CompactionBaseline`.
- `tickCompacting` sets that baseline from the transcript's `compact_boundary` record, which Claude Code writes only after the SessionStart hook finished.
- Transcript times for the cycle: hook output 17:15:49.369–.384, `compact_boundary` 17:15:49.402, typed pointer 17:15:55.340.
  The mark is some 20–30 ms older than the baseline, so `hookDelivered` returns false and the watcher types the pointer.

## Idea

Compare the mark against a time taken before the hook can run, such as the moment the watcher entered the compacting phase or typed `/compact`, instead of the boundary record written after the hook; keep the text match.
A test covers a boundary stamped after the hook's mark.

entries.title: Trial the cuts that make a gate run link fewer new test binaries
entries.brief: Bench the report's cuts on Neve and OSL-1046 before any is made permanent
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/gate-fewer-launches-2026-10-31/report.md` counted the test binaries a gate run links and launches.
Go links one test binary per package per tier, since the tiers select their test files by build tag: 532 on a cold tree, 143 new to the cache on a warm whole-suite run.
On OSL-1046 the endpoint scanner holds each new binary about 10 s, so a change of mean fan-in, about 100 new binaries across three tiers, costs about 1000 s there.
Five packages are imported by every test binary through the shared `TestMain` path (`internal/testkit/tmuxkit`, `internal/proc`, `internal/lymtemp`, `internal/lock`, `internal/agentname`), so a change to one of them rebuilds every binary.

## Idea

Try the report's cuts in practice before any of them is made permanent (operator, 2026-10-31), as a bench in a worktree of its own, measured on OSL-1046 as well as Neve:
- One test binary per package for all tiers, the tier chosen at run time instead of by build tag: the largest saving the report rates medium risk.
- Cut the five universal imports out of the common `TestMain` path: low risk, helps only when one of them changes.
- Merge small leaf test packages into shared binaries within a tier.
- One binary for the whole module per tier is rated high risk, since packages then share one process and Go's per-package test cache is lost; bench it only if the others fall short.

Each trial reports the new binaries and scanner hold it saves and whether the test results stay the same.
